summaries.example: Imagine testing one small piece of cloth to learn about a whole roll. Jevons said reasoning often uses a sample or pattern, but the sample must really match the larger thing. He also used a machine with counters, called a logical abacus, to help sort many possible combinations.
summaries.summary: William Stanley Jevons was a nineteenth-century thinker who worked in logic, mathematics, statistics, and economics. He tried to explain how people reason and how science learns from evidence. He said that rules such as “a thing is itself” and “a thing cannot both be and not be in the same way” are starting points for knowledge. Jevons also believed mathematics should grow out of logic, although later thinkers found problems in parts of his system. His more lasting influence came from using data, averages, probability, and index numbers to study society and markets. In economics, he described choices through usefulness and self-interest and often used simplified “typical” people in his models. The SEP entry also explains that some of his ideas about class, gender, and race were prejudiced, even while he supported improving working people’s lives. Jevons connected science, religion, and evolution in his own Unitarian view.
key_ideas: Jevons studied both philosophy and economics.
He believed basic rules of thought help us tell good reasoning from mistakes.
He connected logic with mathematics and even built a logical abacus.
He used statistics and index numbers to study changes in the economy.
His economic ideas used usefulness, choice, and self-interest, but his views about some groups were shaped by unfair nineteenth-century beliefs.
summaries.why_it_matters: Jevons helps us see how several modern tools grew together: formal logic, economic models, statistics, and the study of evidence. His work also teaches an important lesson about using averages. An average can show a broad pattern, but it may hide how different people are. Studying Jevons means learning both from his useful methods and from the limits and unfair assumptions in some of his social ideas.

important_terms.definition: A careful way of deciding whether an idea or conclusion follows from what we already know.
Learning from observations and examples, then forming a general idea.
A rule that says a thing is itself and not something different at the same time.
A number that helps compare how something changes, such as the value of gold.

questions_to_think_about: When is a small sample a good guide to a larger group?
Can numbers help us understand people without hiding important differences?
Why might a rule for thinking need to be assumed before we can prove anything?
How should we judge useful ideas that are mixed with unfair opinions?

summaries.example: Suppose an economist wants to know whether a rise in wages will make people work more hours. A simple model might predict an answer from self-interest and utility, or usefulness. Jevons's approach shows why that answer may be incomplete: different workers may have different habits, goals, and expectations about the future. A model using a representative individual can be useful for broad analysis, but it cannot automatically settle every question about particular groups.
summaries.summary: William Stanley Jevons was an economist, logician, and philosopher of science whose work anticipated important developments in twentieth-century economics and social statistics. In his account of the laws of thought, identity, contradiction, and the excluded middle are not ordinary discoveries proved from prior reasoning. They are conditions that reasoning and knowledge must already presuppose. His logic sought to express propositions through symbolic combinations of terms, using a principle he called the substitution of similars. He treated deduction as the development and elimination of possibilities, and induction as a more difficult movement from observations toward general scientific claims. Jevons attempted to derive number and mathematics from logical analysis, but the treatment of units raised serious problems, and his formalism did not become a dominant logical system. His empirical work was more influential. He constructed index numbers using a geometric mean to investigate changes in the value of gold and used probability, averages, and data analysis in social inquiry. In economics, he analyzed exchange through utility and self-interest, often using highly rational and foresighted agents. Yet he also recognized that aggregate patterns can coexist with individual diversity. The SEP entry presents a tension in his thought: he supported education and improvement in working-class conditions, but his accounts of class, gender, and race relied on prejudiced assumptions. His Unitarian religious outlook and evolutionary commitments led him to see science and religion as compatible and to support some forms of intervention aimed at moral and social development.
key_ideas: Jevons regarded fundamental laws of thought as objective preconditions for knowledge rather than conclusions proved by reasoning.
His formal logic represented terms and their combinations symbolically and emphasized replacing similar terms in valid inference.
He attempted to ground mathematics in logic, but difficulties in his account of units and criticism from contemporaries limited the system.
His use of index numbers, probability, averages, and empirical data helped anticipate later statistical and econometric methods in social science.
His economic theory abstracted from individual differences, while his discussions of character and groups revealed the limits and prejudices of that abstraction.
He joined economics with utilitarian ideas and connected science, evolution, religion, and proposals for social improvement.
summaries.why_it_matters: Jevons's career illustrates the mixed character of intellectual progress. His formal logic had important limitations, yet his interest in empirical evidence, index numbers, probability, and aggregate behavior helped shape later approaches to economics and statistics. He also raises a continuing methodological question: how far can abstract models explain social life when people differ in motives, opportunities, and circumstances? Finally, the entry shows why historical analysis should examine both a thinker's achievements and the assumptions embedded in them. Technical tools may remain valuable even when the social interpretations attached to them require criticism.

important_terms.definition: The study of correct reasoning and the rules by which conclusions follow from premises.
Reasoning from observed cases toward a broader proposition; Jevons treated it as central to scientific knowledge.
A reasoning process that begins with general premises and derives more specific conclusions.
The usefulness or satisfaction associated with an option, especially in Jevons's economic theory of choice.
A constructed model of a typical participant used to analyze broad economic behavior, not a claim that every person behaves identically.
A numerical measure designed to track changes in a quantity, such as the value of gold or prices over time.
A computed value that summarizes many observations; Jevons distinguished such an average from a definite existing quantity.
A nineteenth-century religious tradition that Jevons associated with rational inquiry, one God, and moral improvement.

questions_to_think_about: If the rules used to prove an argument are already needed for proof, what kind of justification can those rules receive?
When does an average reveal a social pattern, and when can it conceal important differences among groups?
What are the advantages and risks of using a representative individual in economic theory?
Can a scientific model be useful even when its assumptions about people are unrealistic?
How should historical contributions be assessed when technical achievements coexist with prejudiced social judgments?

summaries.example: A school might ask how much time students spend reading each week. The average could show a general pattern, but it might hide the difference between students who read every day and students who read a lot only once in a while. Jevons thought averages could help us understand large groups, while also recognizing that a specific question may require attention to different kinds of people.
summaries.summary: William Stanley Jevons was a philosopher and economist who worked across logic, mathematics, statistics, and social policy. He argued that science depends on basic laws of thought. These include the idea that each thing is itself, that something cannot both be and not be in the same way, and that it must either be or not be. Because these rules are already needed for any proof, Jevons did not think they could be proved in the usual way. He also developed a symbolic system of logic and used a mechanical logical abacus to handle combinations of terms. His attempt to base mathematics on logic had weaknesses, especially in explaining what a counted unit is. Jevons's work with evidence was especially important. He created index numbers while studying the changing value of gold and used probability, averages, and data to investigate economic and social patterns. In economics, he emphasized utility and self-interest and often reasoned with a model of a typical person. He understood that large groups may show regular patterns even though individuals differ greatly. The entry also discusses his Unitarian religious outlook and his belief that evolution and science could fit with religion. At the same time, his writing included harmful assumptions about social groups, even though he favored efforts to improve working-class conditions.
key_ideas: Jevons thought some basic thinking rules must be accepted before science or proof can begin.
He described three basic laws: a thing is itself, a thing cannot both be and not be in the same way, and a thing must either be or not be.
He used symbols to study logic and tried to connect logic with mathematics.
He made important early uses of statistics and index numbers in studying economic changes.
He believed averages can reveal patterns in large groups, but particular groups may need separate attention.
His economic and social writing combined useful analysis with views about race, gender, and class that reflect serious nineteenth-century prejudice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Jevons connects questions that still matter: How do we reason correctly? How should evidence be used? When does a model help us understand people, and when does it oversimplify them? His work shows why statistics can be powerful but must be interpreted carefully. It also reminds us to examine the values and assumptions behind theories, not just the neatness of their equations or the usefulness of their results.

important_terms.definition: Rules for deciding whether a conclusion is supported by the information before us.
Reasoning from examples or observations to a wider rule.
Reasoning from a general rule to a particular conclusion.
The benefit or satisfaction a person expects from a choice.
A number used to compare changes over time, such as changes in prices or the value of gold.
A single calculated result used to describe many pieces of information.
A simplified model of a typical person in an economic theory.

questions_to_think_about: Why can’t we prove every rule of reasoning by using reasoning?
What might an average tell us, and what might it leave out?
Why would an economist use a simplified model of a person?
Should evidence from a large group always guide decisions about one person?
What can we learn from a thinker whose work contains both valuable ideas and biased assumptions?
